correlates.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
correlates.presentation: Sudden choking or coughing followed by unilateral wheeze, decreased breath sounds, and reduced expansion on the affected side.
correlates.pathophysiology: The right mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left, so gravity and airflow carry aspirated material preferentially down the right side (Slide 9).

correlates.name: Tracheoesophageal Fistula (Congenital)
correlates.presentation: A neonatal anomaly; feeds and secretions cross into the airway.
correlates.pathophysiology: Failure of the tracheoesophageal septum to completely separate the respiratory diverticulum from the foregut leaves a persistent connection between the trachea and the esophagus.

correlates.name: Sickle Cell Anemia in the Pulmonary Bed
correlates.presentation: Respiratory manifestations of the disease follow from obstruction of this bed.
correlates.pathophysiology: Pulmonary capillaries admit red cells essentially one at a time and depend on the cell deforming to fit a ~6 micrometer lumen. A misshapen, rigid cell cannot deform and lodges, obstructing the bed (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Pneumothorax and Loss of Pleural Pressure
correlates.presentation: Failure of ventilation on the affected side.
correlates.pathophysiology: Ventilation depends on the pressure differential between parietal and visceral pleura, not on chest wall mechanics alone.

correlates.name: Pleural Effusion and Thoracocentesis
correlates.presentation: Aspiration of the fluid for analysis; ultrasound is increasingly used to localize it.
correlates.pathophysiology: Fluid collects by gravity in the costodiaphragmatic recess, the largest region of pleural cavity without lung in it (Slide 26).
correlates.treatment: Pleural tap in the 8th or 9th intercostal space, midaxillary line, just superior to the superior border of the rib (Slide 32).
